releases.title: Suggest player control improvements
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Your ideas would make each protagonist’s phone feel like a personal possession, with details that reveal their relationships before a conversation even starts. I’d build on that with a clear distinction between **the protagonist’s starting setup** and **what the player can change afterward**.

For your existing ideas, I’d suggest:

- **Protagonist-specific home screens:** Give each protagonist a predetermined wallpaper, app arrangement, colour theme, and lock screen. Their starting choices can hint at their personality or history.
- **Fixed device proportions:** Let players choose phone or tablet mode and adjust the overall scale while preserving that mode’s aspect ratio. Include a “fit to screen” control.
- **Editable contact names:** Start with names that reflect each protagonist’s relationships—“Mum,” “Dr. Vale,” “Alex,” or an old nickname. Player edits should persist without changing the character’s underlying identity.
- **Separate contact names from dialogue:** Renaming someone in the phone should affect their contact card, notifications, and conversation header. Whether it changes how the protagonist addresses them in messages should be a separate choice.

Other improvements I’d consider:

**Personal touches**

- **Contact photos and favourites.** Let players choose from unlocked photos, pin conversations, and mark favourite contacts. Start each protagonist with a different selection.
- **Unlockable wallpapers with story meaning.** Photos received during conversations or taken during important moments become optional backgrounds. Keep the original protagonist wallpaper available.
- **Individual notification sounds.** Assign a tone or vibration pattern to important contacts so players can recognise who messaged before looking.
- **Personal notes.** A small notes app where players can write theories, reminders, or observations alongside clearly distinguished story-created entries.
- **Optional relationship details.** Contact cards could show birthdays, shared photos, and facts learned through play, without reducing relationships to visible affection scores.

**Phone and navigation controls**

- **Consistent back behaviour.** Back or Escape should close the current overlay, then return to the previous screen, then the home screen. A visible home button should always be available.
- **Remember where you were.** Reopening a conversation restores its scroll position, with a “jump to newest” button when messages arrive.
- **Unread navigation.** Add an unread filter and a subtle indicator when new messages arrive in another conversation.
- **Search message history.** Search by contact or phrase, with results limited to messages the player has already seen.
- **Comfortable input options.** Support mouse, keyboard, and touch where available. Make text size independent of device scale, so a smaller phone window can still be readable.
- **Clear reply confirmation.** Highlight a selected response before sending, with an optional confirm step to prevent accidental story choices.

**Player comfort and story flow**

- **Adjustable message pacing.** Separate settings for text reveal speed and simulated typing delays, including an instant option.
- **Notification privacy.** Choose full previews, sender-only previews, or a simple “new message” indicator on the lock screen.
- **Reduced motion and sound controls.** Independently adjust screen animations, vibration effects, notification sounds, and background audio.
- **Safe cosmetic previews.** Preview wallpapers, colours, and contact changes before applying them, with a reset to the protagonist’s defaults.
- **Separate settings by scope.** Keep contact names, wallpaper, and pinned chats within each playthrough; keep accessibility and control preferences shared across the game.

My strongest additional suggestion is **a believable starting phone history for each protagonist**: a few old messages, existing photos, saved notes, and differently named contacts. Combined with your wallpapers, that makes choosing a protagonist feel like stepping into a different life—not just changing the name on the same phone.

releases.title: Review Mysterious Hearts save system
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Yes. The system already has a good foundation: atomic file replacement, five rotating backups, named saves, and automatic archiving before a new story.

After reviewing the code, I’d prioritize these improvements:

1. **Prevent closing after a failed save.** Currently, a save failure displays an error, but closing still destroys the window. Make saving return success/failure, and keep the story open if it fails. This is the most important fix. [game.py](/C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game%20Creator/game.py:1223)

2. **Keep backups across meaningful time intervals.** The five backups rotate whenever saved content changes, so frequent actions can replace every recovery point quickly. Keep recent backups alongside checkpoints from earlier sessions and the start of each game day. [qol.py](/C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game%20Creator/qol.py:9)

3. **Offer recovery directly when Continue fails.** Check backups for loadable stories and offer the newest valid one, showing its date and progress. Preserve the damaged file for possible recovery.

4. **Protect each playthrough separately.** Named saves currently act as snapshots, while playing continues into one shared autosave. Give each story its own autosave and backup history so switching stories cannot gradually displace another story’s recovery points.

5. **Make the save library easier to recognize.** Show protagonist, in-game date, location, turn count, and last saved time. Clearly distinguish named saves from automatic backups. [qol_ui.py](/C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game%20Creator/qol_ui.py:25)

6. **Strengthen compatibility checks.** Add explicit save migrations and validate nested data before loading. Some malformed saves can currently produce unexpected exceptions rather than a clear recovery message. [game_core.py](/C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game%20Creator/game_core.py:342)

I’d tackle **failed-save protection, longer-lived backups, and guided recovery first**. Those provide the biggest protection for an ongoing story. No files changed.

releases.title: Suggest simulation improvements
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Agreed—**sending messages should be independent of waiting for replies**, so you can text Emily, switch to Sophie, send another message, then return when either responds.

I’d make it work like this:

- **Each chat has its own pending messages and response state.** Switching chats doesn’t cancel a reply or block sending elsewhere.
- **Message bursts appear as separate bubbles.** Characters can send a short sequence when it suits their voice; players can send several messages before receiving an answer.
- **Characters respond to what they’ve actually read.** Messages arriving before they begin composing can be considered together. A message sent after that point remains available for a subsequent response.
- **Replies arrive in the background**, with unread badges and a notification. They don’t force you into that conversation.
- **Ordering stays consistent within each chat.** An older generation can’t overwrite a newer exchange or mark unseen messages as read.

The AI requests can still run through a queue—particularly for the local model—while the interface remains usable. Multiple conversations can be awaiting replies even if the model generates only one at a time.

Crucially, **“typing” should mean the character is composing**, rather than merely waiting in the AI queue. Their simulated availability determines when they read and respond; generation supplies the wording.

This also means removing the current global response lock and saving outgoing messages immediately. A failed response would affect only that chat, with your sent messages preserved and the rest of the phone still usable.

releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Yes—**double texting should be a character decision, rather than a fixed reminder timer.** It would make messaging feel much more natural, especially alongside delivered/read states and activity-based replies.

The player should be able to send another message while the first is unread or unanswered. Each message keeps its own timestamp and receipt status. When the character eventually responds, they can address the messages together, rather than producing a separate reply to every bubble.

For NPCs, follow-up timing and likelihood should depend on:

- **Conversation context:** an imminent meeting warrants a quicker follow-up than a casual observation.
- **Personality:** some characters add thoughts in several short messages; others prefer to wait.
- **Relationship:** familiarity can make spontaneous follow-ups more comfortable, without automatically making characters demanding.
- **Current state:** excitement might prompt another thought; low social battery might discourage initiating.
- **Message status:** unread and read-but-unanswered are different situations, but neither should automatically imply rejection.
- **New developments:** a change of plans, something they just noticed, or an update to their earlier message gives them a reason to text again.

I’d distinguish three behaviours:

| Behaviour | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Message burst** | Several bubbles forming one thought, sent close together |
| **Follow-up** | Revisits an unanswered question or ongoing plan |
| **New initiation** | Starts another topic even though an earlier message remains unanswered |

That distinction matters: someone sending you a funny observation hours later isn’t necessarily chasing a reply.

**The simulation should decide whether and why they text; the AI should write the actual message.** Give it their voice, recent conversation, relevant memories, current activity and the reason for reaching out. It shouldn’t be instructed to always mention your silence, apologise, or ask a question. Sometimes a follow-up is just an extra detail.

There should still be quiet limits behind the scenes: cooldowns, a small unanswered-message budget, and reduced likelihood after repeated unanswered attempts. Those limits can vary by character and circumstance. Sleeping characters won’t send follow-ups, and an explicit “I’m busy, talk tomorrow” should normally postpone them.

One important detail: **delivered/read indicators don’t reveal why someone hasn’t answered.** Characters shouldn’t magically know the player is asleep or upset unless they were told or have another credible source.

I’d replace the current fixed one-follow-up-after-24/48-hours rule with this system. It would support spontaneous, AI-written messages while keeping each character’s initiative believable and avoiding a phone full of repetitive reminders.

releases.title: Suggest simulation improvements
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Yes—these additions would make time and availability matter for both the player and the other characters.

And absolutely: **that apology was only an example, not a response template.** A delayed reply should use the character’s voice, the actual messages, their circumstances and how much time passed. Sometimes they explain the delay; sometimes they simply answer. They shouldn’t automatically apologise or repeat a stock phrase.

I’d structure the additions like this:

| Feature | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Wait 10 minutes** | Advances the world, including journeys, NPC decisions and pending replies |
| **Wait until morning** | Advances to the next 08:00; shows the destination date and time before confirming |
| **Nap — 1 hour** | Advances one hour and restores some energy |
| **Sleep — 8 hours** | Advances eight hours from the current time, including across midnight |
| **Player meters** | Energy, social battery and happiness, using the same underlying rules as NPCs |

**Waiting and sleeping should be different.** Waiting passes time without providing sleep recovery. Sleeping restores energy while the world continues: characters finish work, visit friends, send messages and go to bed themselves. Ordinary incoming texts shouldn’t interrupt sleep.

For the meters, I’d label the sleep-related one **Energy**, so a higher value clearly means better rested:

- **Energy:** falls with waking time and exertion; recovers through sleep. A nap helps without being equivalent to a full night.
- **Social battery:** falls with demanding interactions and recovers through downtime. Comfortable company can be less draining, or restorative.
- **Happiness:** changes gradually through enjoyable activities, connection, accomplishments and difficult experiences. It should remain distinct from momentary emotion.

For the player, those meters should influence activity benefits and available suggestions while **leaving their dialogue and feelings under their control**. Low social battery shouldn’t force a rude response, and low happiness shouldn’t make the narrator declare emotions the player hasn’t chosen.

The messages app should distinguish:

- **Sending:** the message hasn’t entered the game’s message system yet.
- **Delivered:** it reached the recipient’s phone, but they haven’t checked it.
- **Read:** they actually checked the conversation.
- **Typing:** they’re actively composing a reply, when appropriate.

**Read must not mean “a reply is immediately coming.”** Someone can check a message during a work break and answer later. Sleeping characters leave new messages delivered until they wake and check their phone. Opening the messages list shouldn’t automatically mark every conversation read.

One important implementation change: **sending a text must save independently of generating its eventual reply**. That lets you send something, leave the phone, nap or do another activity, and receive the answer later. If AI generation fails, the delivered message stays intact and retrying doesn’t send it twice.

The current midnight stop would also need updating so an eight-hour sleep can cross into the next day correctly. Any appointments crossed during waiting or sleeping should follow their normal attendance rules, with a warning about known commitments before a long skip.

Together, these systems would make a character’s silence understandable—and give the player useful things to do while waiting.

releases.title: Suggest simulation improvements
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
I think this would make the characters feel considerably more independent. **Sleep, availability and response timing should all come from the same simulation**, so their messages match what they’re actually doing.

One refinement: separate **activity** from **location**. “At home” doesn’t necessarily mean available—a character could be asleep, studying or hosting friends there.

| Activity status | Suggested messaging behaviour |
|---|---|
| Asleep | Queues messages until after waking |
| At work / studying | Replies during breaks or after finishing; occasional brief replies if appropriate |
| Free time | Usually responds soon, depending on interest and social energy |
| Socialising | Replies less frequently, especially during an involved activity |
| Travelling | Delays replies while driving |
| Winding down | May reply briefly, say goodnight, then stop responding |

These would be **in-game delays**, separate from the time the AI takes to generate a response.

**Sleep schedules should have a normal bedtime, a wake time and a flexibility window.** Circumstances determine how far someone stretches that window: tomorrow’s responsibilities, tiredness, how much they’re enjoying themselves, or whether a friend needs support. Staying up late should have a consequence the following day rather than silently resetting their energy.

During a hangout, that could produce a natural sequence:

- Near bedtime: “I should probably head back soon.”
- Later: they suggest ending the activity or ask about staying over.
- Past their limit: they say goodbye and leave, accounting for travel time home.

They shouldn’t need the player’s permission to leave. If they’re in the player’s travelling party, departure needs an actual way home rather than teleporting.

**Overnight stays would be an excellent extension.** A character could ask because it’s late, the journey is inconvenient, or they want more time together. That should depend on familiarity, comfort, available sleeping arrangements and next-day commitments. Staying over can be completely platonic; it shouldn’t automatically imply intimacy.

An overnight visit should also persist into the morning: they wake at their own time, perhaps join you for breakfast, leave for work, and remember the visit. Sleeping at your home changes their location, not their underlying sleep needs.

For messaging, I’d add a proper **pending-message queue**:

- Sending a message records it immediately.
- The recipient’s activity determines when they can notice and answer it.
- Several messages sent before they respond can receive one coherent reply.
- On waking, they answer when they have a moment, rather than every sleeping character replying at exactly the same minute.
- Their reply reflects when they read the message: “Sorry, I was asleep. Are you still looking for somewhere to eat?”

The crucial gameplay issue is **how the player waits**. Since idle time currently doesn’t advance the world, the phone needs an obvious “Wait 10 minutes” or “Wait until morning” option, alongside continuing other activities. Otherwise delayed replies could feel like the game has stalled.

Also, distinguish what the simulation knows from what the player knows. “Asleep” can be an internal status without always broadcasting someone’s exact activity. The phone might show “Notifications silenced” or their last shared availability.

Your proposed tick system fits this well: **ticks update needs, scheduled times trigger sleep and waking, and events trigger replies or departures**. I’d make availability and queued messages the foundation, then build bedtime negotiations and overnight visits on top.

releases.title: Suggest character profile features
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
**Rei would be Emily’s starting crush, while her anonymous notes follow how her feelings develop.** Her canon establishes where she begins; the simulation determines whether she keeps pursuing Rei, withdraws, or eventually likes someone else.

I’d separate **her current feelings, her willingness to send a note, and the history of notes she’s already sent**. Those can change independently.

| What happens | How her anonymous notes could change |
|---|---|
| Her feelings for Rei deepen | Notes become more personal, frequent, or easier to identify |
| She still likes Rei but feels hurt | She pauses, leaves drafts unsent, or sends something guarded |
| Rei welcomes the anonymous attention | She feels encouraged, though revealing herself may still frighten her |
| Rei asks the sender to stop | She stops pursuing through the app, even if her feelings remain |
| Her feelings fade | Romantic notes stop; she decides whether to explain or leave the thread unresolved |
| She develops feelings for someone else | New notes become possible if those feelings become meaningful and anonymity suits the situation |

**A change in attraction shouldn’t immediately trigger a new confession.** Emily could have a passing interest in someone while still strongly attached to Rei. Sending a romantic note should require sustained feelings, a reason to reach out, and enough willingness to risk being discovered. That keeps her from switching recipients after every positive interaction.

Her existing thread with Rei would retain its history. Earlier confessions were sincere when she wrote them, even if they no longer describe how she feels. She might:

- Quietly stop writing.
- Continue talking but become less romantic.
- Send a goodbye or explain that her feelings have changed.
- Reveal herself to give Rei closure.
- Leave things unresolved because she doesn’t know what to say.

Those choices should reflect Emily’s personality and what happened between them.

For example, Emily sends Rei several affectionate notes, but their in-person relationship gradually becomes distant. Meanwhile, she grows closer to another character through repeated meaningful interactions. She stops drafting notes to Rei before she’s ready to admit why. If Rei later replies, “I miss hearing from you,” that creates a decision: reconnect, explain, or avoid answering. **It shouldn’t automatically restore her old crush.**

Rei’s knowledge stays separate throughout. Rei may notice the notes have stopped without knowing who sent them or why. If Rei discovers Emily’s identity much later, the revelation is **“Emily had feelings for me,”** not necessarily **“Emily still has feelings for me.”**

That distinction gives the notes lasting story value: they preserve a moment in a relationship, while the people involved keep changing.

releases.title: Suggest simulation improvements
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Yes—**a fixed simulation tick would work well for this**, especially with the existing game clock. Your ideas also reinforce each other: a character’s needs motivate an action, their relationships influence whom they approach, and the resulting encounter changes their needs and relationships.

I’d use a **five-minute in-game tick as a starting point**, with characters reconsidering plans every 15–30 minutes or when something meaningful happens. Advancing time through travel, conversation or resting would process the intervening simulation. Real-world idle time would remain paused.

Your three ideas could work like this:

- **Spontaneous visits and hangouts.** Characters decide they want company, choose someone, check their availability and travel there. Close friends might knock unannounced; less familiar people might text first. They need a known address, a plausible reason and enough free time. You can welcome them, suggest somewhere else or say you’re busy. They could also invite other NPCs without involving you.
- **Sleep, social battery and happiness.** These should influence choices rather than dictate them. A tired character can still attend something important, but might leave early. Social battery should be distinct from wanting company: someone can feel lonely while lacking energy for a party, making a quiet visit appealing. Happiness works best as slower overall wellbeing, alongside the existing immediate moods.
- **Meeting new people.** Emily and Valentina could meet through a mutual friend, an event or repeatedly visiting the same place. An actual introduction creates an acquaintance; enjoyable encounters and deliberate follow-up can develop friendship. Shared location alone shouldn’t immediately make them friends.

More additions that would fit:

1. **Different kinds of company meet different needs.**  
   A comfortable friend might make a quiet evening restorative, while a large gathering drains energy. Personality and familiarity determine the effect, so “socialising” isn’t one interchangeable action.

2. **Characters choose specific people for specific reasons.**  
   Someone might seek Samantha for training, April for a thoughtful conversation or Emily for reassurance. Friendship develops a character of its own, beyond a single closeness score.

3. **Invitations spread naturally.**  
   Emily invites you for coffee and asks whether Valentina can come. Friends introduce friends, creating new groups and opportunities for the player to meet people too. Private plans should require agreement before extra guests join.

4. **Visits have an intended activity and a natural ending.**  
   Someone comes over to cook, show you something, unwind or ask for advice. They can suggest changing activities and eventually leave for sleep, work or another commitment. This makes a spontaneous visit feel like an event rather than an indefinitely open chat.

5. **Characters remember whether interactions were rewarding.**  
   Being listened to makes them more likely to seek you out for support. Enjoying a shared activity makes them propose it again. Repeated uncomfortable encounters encourage different plans, without every declined invitation counting as rejection.

6. **Plans can adapt to circumstances.**  
   Rain turns an outdoor outing into cooking together. A tired friend suggests a shorter visit. Someone arriving at an empty café messages another friend or heads elsewhere. Give characters a fallback plan so failed intentions produce believable behaviour.

7. **Friendship is directional.**  
   Emily may consider Valentina a promising new friend while Valentina still sees Emily as a pleasant acquaintance. Track each person’s interest, trust and willingness to initiate separately. Unequal enthusiasm creates variety without needing manufactured conflict.

8. **Small independent life events create conversation.**  
   A character has a difficult shift, discovers a new hobby, receives praise or struggles with a project. These events affect their state and give them reasons to reach out. Keep major developments authored or constrained so random events don’t rewrite canon.

For the simulation itself, I’d separate the timing into three layers:

| Layer | When it runs | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Needs | Every five game minutes | Updates sleep pressure, social energy and wellbeing influences |
| Decisions | When free, periodically, or after a meaningful event | Chooses whether to rest, work, socialise, visit or continue a project |
| Scheduled events | At their recorded times | Handles departures, arrivals, appointments and activity completion |

**Don’t make every character pick a new action every tick.** Once Emily decides to visit Valentina, that intention should persist through messaging, travelling and the visit unless there’s a reason to change it. Otherwise characters will constantly switch plans.

A lightweight scoring system would be enough initially:

> Appeal of an action = need it satisfies + personal preference + relationship interest − effort − conflicts.

Then choose among the strongest valid options with a little controlled randomness. Store the chosen plan and outcome in the save. The AI can write the invitation or conversation when needed; background decisions shouldn’t require an AI request every tick.

**The first version I’d build is needs → choosing company → invitation → travel → hangout → remembered outcome.** That single loop would support both spontaneous player visits and Emily independently becoming friends with Valentina.

releases.body:
That gives Emily a clear character rule: **she can send anonymous romantic confessions to Rei, but never to anyone else.** The simulation can decide when she sends them and how she responds afterward, while respecting that canon.

For Emily and Rei, I’d handle it like this:

- **Emily’s feelings are established; her actions depend on circumstances.** A meaningful moment with Rei might encourage a note. Fear of rejection might make her delay, write vaguely, or abandon a draft.
- **Rei doesn’t automatically know it’s Emily.** Rei interprets the notes using their shared experiences, existing suspicions, and whatever Emily accidentally reveals.
- **Emily remembers exactly what she sent.** If Rei mentions a note, Emily understands the reference and might become nervous, ask what Rei thought, or try to hide her interest.
- **Her clues become personal over time.** Early notes might be general compliments. Later ones could mention something Rei did for her, making the sender easier to identify.
- **Rei can suspect the wrong person.** Emily’s exclusive romantic target is a rule for her behaviour, not information available to Rei.
- **Emily only reacts to misunderstandings she learns about.** If Rei privately suspects someone else, Emily won’t know. If Rei tells her or starts openly pursuing that person, she can react to that evidence.

For example, Emily sends:

> “You probably don’t remember sitting with me when I didn’t want to talk, but I do.”

Rei remembers several people they’ve comforted, so it isn’t proof. Later, Emily brings up that same afternoon using similar wording. Rei can gently ask her about it, reply through the app, or keep wondering.

The relationship effects would stay separate: **Rei might grow attached to the anonymous sender while their relationship with Emily barely changes.** Meanwhile, Emily might feel encouraged by Rei’s anonymous replies, even though Rei hasn’t knowingly reciprocated her feelings toward Emily.

One distinction worth deciding is whether **Rei is the only person Emily can ever develop romantic feelings for**, or simply **the only person she sends anonymous confessions to**. Your example establishes the second rule; the first would be a broader restriction on her romance story.

releases.title: Suggest character profile features
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
I’d build it around **evidence, personal interpretation, and choices**. The player and characters encounter the same kinds of clues, but they can reach different conclusions and act differently.

**1. Every message creates a separate mystery**

The game records the actual sender, while the recipient starts with their own knowledge:

- The message and when it arrived.
- Who might know the details it mentions.
- Familiar phrases, interests, or writing habits.
- Relevant conversations or events they personally experienced.

If a note says, “I wish we’d stayed longer by the lake,” only someone who knows about that evening should connect it to the lake visit. A character who wasn’t there could still know because someone told them—but the game needs to track that information spreading.

Some messages should have very little usable evidence.

**2. Suspicions belong to individuals**

Each recipient has their own possible suspects. Evidence changes how plausible each person seems, without immediately establishing the truth.

| Observation | Possible interpretation |
|---|---|
| Uses an expression Alex often says | Alex becomes more plausible |
| Mentions your favourite dessert | Someone who knows your preferences |
| Describes a private conversation | Someone involved, or someone they told |
| Alex denies sending it | How convincing that feels depends on existing trust |
| Morgan admits sending it | Strong evidence, though false claims can be possible |

Keep **“unknown sender”** as a possibility, so characters don’t automatically settle on the last available suspect.

For the player, I’d show labels such as *possible*, *likely*, and *confirmed*, with supporting and conflicting clues. Let the player choose their main suspect rather than having the game decide their belief.

**3. Investigation happens through social actions**

Both the player and other characters could:

- Reply anonymously and ask a question.
- Ask a friend for their opinion.
- Mention a detail to a suspect and observe their response.
- Ask someone directly.
- Share the message to gather information.
- Wait for more evidence.
- Decide they don’t want to investigate.

Every action has a tradeoff. Asking a friend may help, but now that friend knows about the message. Confronting someone may produce an answer, but it also reveals your suspicion.

Avoid making reactions into perfect lie detectors: nervousness could mean attraction, embarrassment, or discomfort with being accused.

**4. Characters decide whether investigating is worth it**

Characters shouldn’t all investigate every message. Their decisions could depend on:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| Curiosity | More likely to pursue clues |
| Desire for privacy | Less likely to share the message |
| Directness | More likely to ask a suspect outright |
| Fear of rejection | More likely to investigate indirectly |
| Existing attraction | More emotionally invested in certain answers |
| Message importance | A personal confession gets more attention than a casual compliment |

Personality should influence interpretation, too. A hopeful character may favour someone they like; an insecure character may suspect a compliment is a joke. Evidence should still matter, so those biases don’t make their behaviour arbitrary.

**5. Suspicion changes expectations before it changes relationships**

I’d keep *confidence about the sender* separate from attraction, trust, and closeness. Suspecting someone sent a note doesn’t automatically mean liking them more.

Instead, the effect depends on **what the message means to the recipient, how strongly they believe the theory, and what happens next**.

| Situation | Possible relationship effect |
|---|---|
| A welcome confession seems to come from someone they like | Increased romantic interest; more flirting |
| A thoughtful note seems to come from a friend | Feeling understood; greater perceived closeness |
| An intrusive message seems to come from someone | Increased caution or distance |
| A suspect gives a denial the recipient believes | Suspicion decreases; trust may stay intact |
| Someone repeatedly accuses an innocent person | The accused loses trust in the accuser |
| Someone shares a private note widely | The sender may feel exposed and lose trust, if they learn about it |

These effects should be **directional**. Jamie might feel closer to Alex because Jamie thinks Alex sent a lovely message. Alex might simply be confused by Jamie’s sudden affection.

**6. Anonymous relationships need their own emotional history**

The recipient can develop feelings toward the *anonymous sender* separately from feelings toward any suspect.

For example:

> Jamie enjoys talking to the anonymous sender, but suspects it’s Alex. Jamie starts flirting with Alex in person. Later, Morgan reveals they were the sender.

The reveal shouldn’t simply transfer all accumulated attraction to Morgan. Jamie might appreciate Morgan’s kindness, feel disappointed it wasn’t Alex, feel uncomfortable about the secrecy, or need time to reconcile the anonymous conversations with the person they know.

That gives identity reveals emotional weight.

**7. Wrong guesses create consequences through behaviour**

A private mistaken suspicion should usually have modest effects. Acting on it can have much larger ones.

For example:

1. Alex sends Jamie a kind anonymous note.
2. Jamie suspects Morgan and tells a friend.
3. The friend tells Morgan that Jamie thinks Morgan has a crush.
4. Morgan approaches Jamie about it.
5. Alex sees them spending time together but doesn’t know why.

Now everyone has a different understanding of the situation. Alex can become jealous about what they witnessed, but shouldn’t magically know about Jamie’s theory or the friend’s conversation.

For the player, the investigation screen could show **the original message, clues and their sources, suspects, and unresolved questions**. Other characters would keep an equivalent internal record, while the player discovers their theories through conversations and behaviour.

The central rule is: **beliefs influence how people act; those actions—and the meaning people attach to them—change relationships.** That would let the mysteries generate believable social stories without every clue directly adding or subtracting relationship points.

releases.title: Suggest simulation improvements
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Mysterious Hearts already has schedules, travel, moods, relationship bonds, personal projects and character-specific memories. **The biggest improvement would be letting characters make decisions from those systems**, so they feel like people with lives beyond the player.

Here are the additions I’d prioritise:

1. **Characters initiate meaningful plans.**  
   Beyond unanswered-message follow-ups, let characters invite you somewhere, ask for help, share news or revisit an unfinished conversation. Emily could invite you to see her completed window arrangement; Sophie could ask you to time a practice lap. Invitations should offer concrete times and allow declining or rescheduling.

2. **Personal priorities influence daily routines.**  
   Give each character a few competing motivations: responsibilities, rest, social connection and personal ambitions. Sophie might choose recovery after demanding training; Minsu might prioritise study before an assessment. Keep scheduled obligations reliable, with flexible leisure around them.

3. **Projects progress through actual activity.**  
   Currently, the authored projects advance based on elapsed days. Make progress depend on characters finding time, obtaining something they need, or overcoming a small setback. They should still finish things independently, but your involvement could change the process and their memories of it.

4. **NPC friendships develop without you.**  
   Extend shared-location familiarity into purposeful interactions: friends arrange lunch, help with projects, disagree or reconcile. These events should influence their bonds and later conversations. You learn about them through witnessing or disclosure, preserving the existing knowledge boundaries.

5. **Characters negotiate and set boundaries.**  
   An invitation shouldn’t always be a simple yes/no or automatic attendance. Characters could suggest another time, prefer a different venue, leave when tired, or ask for a private conversation. High affection should coexist with their own commitments and preferences.

6. **Emotions have causes and recovery paths.**  
   Connect feelings to remembered events, with an intensity and duration. A stressful shift might make someone quieter; finishing a project might lift their mood. An apology could ease hurt without instantly restoring trust. Dialogue should distinguish “having a bad day” from “upset with you.”

7. **Promises become opportunities for follow-through.**  
   Build on the commitment ledger: characters remember an agreed favour, prepare for it, ask about it when relevant, and acknowledge completion. Keep a clear distinction between a suggestion, an accepted plan and a promise. Avoid punishing the player for ambiguous dialogue.

8. **Relationships develop individual habits.**  
   Expand the existing shared rituals into character-initiated traditions: a regular café visit, post-training food or exchanging sketches. Characters could remember your usual activity and propose a variation. This makes closeness visible through behaviour rather than just rising numbers.

**I’d start with meaningful invitations, flexible priorities and activity-based project progress.** Together, they create a noticeable loop: a character wants something, makes time for it, acts independently, and involves you when it makes sense.

For implementation, let the simulation decide actions and record outcomes, then let the AI express them in character. Use the existing game clock, persist decisions across saves, and limit unsolicited messages so autonomy feels lively rather than demanding.

releases.title: Suggest character profile features
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
I think this could be a defining feature of *Mysterious Hearts*. It gives the title a place inside the world and creates a natural connection between romance, secrets, and investigation. **Characters sending messages to each other is especially valuable**: relationships can develop without the player initiating every event.

The most important design rule would be **separating what happened from what each character knows**. The simulation knows the sender, but the recipient only has their message and whatever evidence they discover. Other characters shouldn’t know about it unless someone tells them, shows them, or they witness something.

A few systems could make that work particularly well:

- **Messages with different intentions.** Confessions, compliments, apologies, warnings, questions, jealousy, or attempts to repair a friendship. Each should come from the sender’s personality and current relationships.
- **Anonymous conversation threads.** Recipients can reply while the sender remains anonymous. This creates situations where someone becomes emotionally close to a person whose identity they don’t know.
- **Clues through ordinary interaction.** Wording, favourite songs, an inside joke, or knowledge of a particular event can suggest a sender. These should be clues with multiple possible explanations, rather than instant answers.
- **Character-specific suspicions.** Each person develops their own theories and confidence levels. A suspicious character might jump to conclusions; a cautious one might wait for evidence.
- **Ways to investigate socially.** Ask friends, bring up a detail from the message, compare stories, or directly ask a suspect. Investigating should sometimes change the relationship even when the guess is wrong.
- **Choices around revealing yourself.** Senders can confess, leave another clue, deny involvement, or remain anonymous. Recipients can welcome the attention, ignore it, ask for honesty, or block the thread.
- **Consequences for sharing messages.** Showing a private confession to a friend might help identify the sender, but spreading it could damage trust. Characters should also make those decisions themselves.
- **Different attitudes toward anonymity.** One character finds it romantic, another finds it frustrating, and another only uses the app because they’re too shy to speak openly.

For example: **Alex sends Jamie an anonymous note about a song they heard together. Jamie suspects Morgan and asks Morgan about it. Morgan takes that as romantic interest. Alex notices them getting closer and becomes jealous.** That’s a story emerging from a single message—but each reaction needs to follow what the characters actually know.

I’d connect it to the contacts app with a **private investigation section**: messages, possible senders, clues, and your own suspicions. Confirmed identities should be clearly distinct from guesses.

One thing I’d avoid is making every anonymous message a puzzle you’re expected to solve. Some should remain sweet, awkward, unresolved, or deliberately private. **Choosing whether to investigate should matter as much as discovering the sender.**

releases.title: Suggest character profile features
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
The contacts app could become a place where players gradually discover who each character is. Alongside **attraction, trust, closeness, favourites, and your own “About Me” section**, I’d suggest:

- **Details revealed through conversations.** Profiles begin sparse and fill in as characters share things. A favourite movie might appear after a late-night conversation, giving players a reason to remember what people say.
- **Public profile and private notes.** Separate what characters write about themselves from what the player learns. Their bio might say “I love going out,” while your notes reveal they actually prefer quiet nights with close friends.
- **Shared memories.** A small timeline of meaningful moments: your first conversation, an inside joke, an argument, or a promise. Let players pin their favourites.
- **Likes, dislikes, and boundaries.** Beyond favourite foods, include how they feel about surprises, teasing, affection, personal questions, and social situations. These details can make choices feel more personal.
- **Communication style.** Reveal whether they prefer calls or texts, reply in bursts, use voice notes, or need time before discussing difficult topics.
- **Dynamic bios and statuses.** Characters change their profile picture, song, or status as the story progresses. A cryptic status could hint at something the player hasn’t discovered yet.
- **Promises and plans.** Track things you agreed to do together, such as watching a movie or meeting somewhere. Remembering—or forgetting—could affect the relationship.
- **Relationship milestones.** Show meaningful developments such as “Opened up to you,” “Shared a secret,” or “Trust rebuilding.” These give emotional context to the relationship meters.
- **Photo and keepsake collections.** Save pictures they send, gifts exchanged, and little mementos, each with a short description of its significance.
- **Mystery notes.** For *Mysterious Hearts*, let players record unanswered questions or conflicting details. Keep these as observations rather than automatically exposing whether someone is lying.
- **Your own profile affecting interactions.** Characters could notice your favourite music, suggest your favourite food, or comment when you change your bio. Your profile becomes part of the story rather than just a settings screen.
- **Visibility controls for your profile.** Let players choose which personal details they share. Revealing something private to a particular character could become a meaningful moment.

For **attraction, trust, and closeness**, I’d keep them independent: someone can be attracted to you without trusting you, or feel deeply close to you as a friend. If those meters represent the *other character’s* feelings, consider showing descriptive hints until those feelings become clear through the story.

My strongest starting set would be **gradually discovered details, shared memories, changing statuses, and characters reacting to your profile**. Those features would make the contacts app feel connected to the relationships themselves.

Yes. After reviewing the project, I think **the biggest opportunity is making Winterfield visibly respond to daily life and player history**. You already have substantial lore, schedules, holidays, social bonds, and character memory.

These updates would add the most:

| Update | How it would improve immersion |
|---|---|
| **Weather and changing light** | Give locations morning, evening, and night appearances, with persistent weather shared by the map, scenes, and dialogue. Rain could move a café meeting indoors or change a boathouse outing. Current backgrounds are static. |
| **Characters pursuing their own small stories** | Give residents ongoing concerns: Emily preparing an arrangement, Sophie approaching a meet, or Minsu juggling an assignment and training. These progress over several days, with opportunities to help or simply ask how things went. |
| **Places that remember you** | Maya learns your actual order; Mario asks for a verdict on a revised slice; a drawing you made remains on the Bijou wall. Your existing factual memory system provides a useful foundation. |
| **More varied routines** | Add occasional errands, rehearsals, visits, and quiet days. The six hidden residents currently share the same broad work–park–home pattern; individual routines would make discovering them more rewarding. |
| **Local news with visible consequences** | A campus noticeboard, harbour bulletin, and cinema programme could reflect authored events. Let players notice preparations before an occasion and its aftermath afterward. Keep rumours attributed and private knowledge limited to its sources. |
| **Relationship rituals and follow-through** | Let actual repeated experiences become traditions: a favourite table, a shared film night, or an inside joke. Characters could follow up on an unfinished conversation or a promise without treating every exchange as a romance milestone. |
| **A clearer everyday identity for 2050** | Establish a few consistent details about transport, university life, technology, and the waterfront. The setting names 2050, but its everyday texture could make that year feel more deliberate. |
| **Small authored mystery episodes** | Expand the Charles investigation through bounded leads with meaningful outcomes. Each episode should resolve a question, complicate another, and allow ordinary life between discoveries. |

**I’d start with changing light/weather, places remembering you, and character mini-stories.** Together, they would make the town feel different when you return and give conversations something new to grow from—without needing a larger cast or more locations.

One particularly worthwhile social improvement: replace the current automatic sharing of betrayal knowledge with **discovery through witnesses, disclosures, or messages**. Consequences would still matter, but characters would react for understandable reasons.

releases.title: Suggest game QOL improvements
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Yes—**a more structured memory system could improve consistency and reduce response time together.** The game already saves transcripts, relationship milestones, and witnessed memories, but some important information still depends on a repeatedly rewritten summary.

From the current code, I’d prioritise these changes:

**1. Give important events permanent, structured records**

Record each meaningful event with its date, location, participants, actual witnesses, outcome, and supporting conversation.

For example: “Emily and Rei attended the café outing” should be separate from “Rei invited Emily.” Currently, scheduled events and conversation memory are separate systems; scheduling or joining an event doesn’t automatically create a corresponding witnessed memory.

Track events through **planned → attended → completed / cancelled / missed**, so characters remember what actually happened.

**2. Separate facts, memories, and beliefs**

Each character should have distinct records for:

- Established facts: preferences, disclosed personal details, relationship milestones.
- Shared experiences: conversations, outings, gifts, arguments.
- Open commitments: promises, unanswered questions, future plans.
- Beliefs: something another character claimed, which might be uncertain.

Include **who knows each fact and how they learned it**. That prevents private conversations from becoming town-wide knowledge and stops a character’s speculation becoming permanent truth.

**3. Make summaries replaceable, not authoritative**

The current model rewrites a relationship summary under 150 words each turn, and that replaces the previous summary. Important details can gradually disappear or change.

Keep the underlying facts and events permanently. Generate summaries from those records periodically, with source references. Corrections should supersede an incorrect memory while preserving the original history.

**4. Retrieve relevant memories more intelligently**

Current recall primarily uses word overlap and returns up to five memories. Improve selection using the people involved, topic, location, emotional importance, and unfinished commitments.

Always include critical relationship facts and relevant promises—even when the player doesn’t repeat the exact original words. An indexed search would also avoid repeatedly scanning every transcript. These limitations are visible in [character_memory.py](</C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game Creator/character_memory.py>).

**5. Remove duplicated generation work**

This is the clearest response-time opportunity: the first AI request generates suggested replies, then a second request generates them again in the protagonist’s voice.

I’d keep the specialised reply pass initially, but stop requesting disposable choices in the first pass. Then compare that against an optional single-pass mode using actual character-quality tests. The two passes currently run sequentially in [game_core.py](</C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game Creator/game_core.py>).

**6. Generate optional suggestions only when needed**

Generate the main four replies first. Generate personal-talk options when that panel opens, and physical actions only where applicable. Allow custom replies once the character’s response has been validated and committed.

Any unfinished suggestion request would need a turn identifier so it cannot attach outdated choices to a newer conversation.

**7. Send smaller, more focused prompts**

The current prompts contain extensive repeated rules, world details, and relationship context. Supply a compact package containing:

- Stable character identity and voice
- Current scene and authoritative relationship state
- Relevant memories and outstanding commitments
- A short recent conversation history

Keep stable instructions together to make prompt reuse possible where the provider supports it. This should be measured rather than assuming a particular speedup.

**8. Prioritise conversation requests and measure delays**

Use one request queue that prioritises player conversations over Grove posts and optional suggestions. Grove avoids starting work while the game is busy, but an already-running request can still compete.

Measure prompt preparation, provider wait, generation, validation retries, reply generation, and saving separately. That will show where optimisation actually helps.

**My recommended order:** connect scheduled events to permanent memories, add structured facts and promises, remove duplicate reply generation, then optimise retrieval and prompts. Keep the existing JSON saves initially; changing storage format alone won’t improve character memory or model speed.

releases.title: Suggest game QOL improvements
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Looking through the current game, **the biggest QOL gains would come from making conversations, travel, and returning to a save smoother.** You already have maps, journals, calendars, unread indicators, and retry controls, so I’d build on those.

1. **Multiple save slots and automatic backups**  
   Keep separate Garrett, Rei, and Minsu playthroughs, name saves, and restore a recent autosave. This would be a big improvement over the current single story save.

2. **A “While you were away” recap**  
   When continuing, show your last conversation, current location, active date goals, and upcoming events. Keep it grounded in recorded events so it doesn’t invent history.

3. **Better handling of AI wait times**  
   Show whether the game is generating the character’s response or preparing your reply choices, with an elapsed timer and Cancel button. Ideally, display the character’s finished message while suggested replies are still loading.

4. **Persistent drafts for each conversation**  
   Remember unfinished texts separately for every contact, including after closing the phone or restarting. Preserve scroll position when switching conversations, too.

5. **Searchable conversation history**  
   Search by character, phrase, or day across texts and hangouts. Let players bookmark memorable messages and jump directly to their original context.

6. **Travel previews and useful shortcuts**  
   Before driving, show arrival time and whether the person you want to meet is expected to still be there. Add favourite destinations and a “Go home” shortcut.

7. **Clear action costs and unavailable-button explanations**  
   Label actions with their time and money costs: “Work · 45 min · +$4,000.” Explain blocked actions directly: “Available from 20:00” or “Meet in person to give this gift.”

8. **An optional relationship-change feed**  
   Briefly show changes such as “Trust +2 · You offered support.” Keep this optional for players who prefer a more immersive experience without visible scoring.

9. **A compact daily agenda**  
   Bring today’s birthdays, planned dates, unfinished date goals, and available work into one panel. Offer a gentle reminder before finishing the day.

10. **Reading and accessibility settings**  
    Adjustable text size, UI scaling, reduced animation, separate sound controls, and keyboard shortcuts for reply choices—with shortcuts disabled while typing.

**My first three would be save slots, better AI waiting controls, and persistent conversation drafts.** Those would remove everyday friction without needing to expand the story or change the characters.

- The server runs the game; your PC can be off.
- You play through your phone’s browser.
- Eligible AI requests use your ChatGPT plan, without a separate API key.
- Mobile saves stay separate from your desktop saves.
- You’d pay for server hosting, and ChatGPT usage limits still apply.

The documented setup requires initial sign-in locally, followed by securely transferring that app’s authorization to your server. We’d need to adapt and test the existing integration.

**If you also want no server hosting, a standalone HTML file isn’t a supported way to retain the current ChatGPT-powered dialogue.** We’d need a different approach, such as scripted dialogue or an on-device model.

releases.title: Generate ElevenLabs prompts
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
These are **20 ready-to-paste voice design prompts** based on your character profiles. Garrett has a British accent; everyone else has an American accent. Pitch and vocal texture are proposed choices to make the cast sound distinct.

**1. Garrett Han**
> A 22-year-old man with a contemporary Southern English British accent. Warm, resonant mid-low pitch with a lightly textured edge. Relaxed, charismatic and shamelessly confident, with smiling vowels, effortless flirtation and impeccable timing for cheeky comebacks. Conversational pacing, never rushed. His swagger can soften into sincere, understated warmth or become quiet and deliberate when serious. Natural, intimate dialogue with clear studio-quality audio.

**2. Rei Takamura**
> A 21-year-old man with a neutral American accent. Low-mid pitch, smooth and slightly smoky, with restrained resonance and clear articulation. Reserved, observant and quietly self-assured. Short phrases, unhurried pacing and comfortable pauses. Deadpan humour lands as an ordinary statement, sometimes a beat late. Subtle warmth emerges around people he trusts. Emotionally nuanced rather than flat or monotonous. Natural conversational delivery with clean studio-quality audio.

**3. Yuriko Takamura**
> An 18-year-old adult woman with a neutral American accent. Bright, clear mid-high pitch with a lightly textured, expressive tone. Curious, inventive and wry, with quick changes in inflection and playful, practical teasing. Her pace picks up when explaining a creative idea, then settles when she wants someone to listen closely. Youthful but distinctly adult, confident in her own opinions. Natural dialogue with clean studio-quality audio.

**4. April Xu**
> A 21-year-old woman with a neutral American accent. Clear mid-range pitch, smooth texture and precise, effortless articulation. Measured pacing with economical emphasis and beautifully timed pauses before a dry correction. Composed, intelligent and observant, with understated warmth beneath her reserve. Amusement appears as a subtle smile in the voice. Allow small breaks in composure during sincere moments. Natural and human, with clean studio-quality audio.

**5. Ivan Yeun**
> A 24-year-old man with a neutral American accent. A polished, velvety low-mid speaking voice with balanced resonance and a musician’s precise sense of rhythm. Calm, assured and quietly magnetic. Crisp consonants, relaxed phrasing and understated dry wit. Offstage conversation feels intimate and unforced. Under pressure, his delivery becomes shorter and more controlled. Warmth is subtle but unmistakable. Spoken dialogue, with clean studio-quality audio.

**6. Minsu Park**
> A 19-year-old adult man with a neutral American accent. Bright mid-range pitch with warm resonance and a lively, clear tone. Outgoing, spontaneous and approachable, with buoyant inflection and easy conversational humour. Moderately quick pacing that slows naturally when listening or offering thoughtful reassurance. His enthusiasm feels attentive and grounded, with a smile frequently audible in his voice. Youthful, distinctly adult delivery with clean studio-quality audio.

**7. Emily Fields**
> A 20-year-old adult woman with a neutral American accent. Soft, warm mid-high pitch with gentle breathiness and clear, delicate articulation. Shy, sincere and quietly expressive. A natural intermittent stutter appears through occasional brief initial-sound repetitions or phrase restarts, especially when surprised or emotionally exposed; allow fluent sentences too. More animated when discussing her interests, quietly firm when stating a boundary. Adult, never childlike. Close, clean studio-quality audio.

**8. Sophie Parker**
> A 21-year-old woman with a neutral American accent. Bright mid-range pitch with an athletic, lightly husky edge and strong vocal clarity. Brisk, confident phrasing, playful challenges and quick, cheeky timing. Energetic and adventurous, with spontaneous laughter and lively emphasis. Her competitiveness comes through as engaging enthusiasm. During vulnerable moments, the pace slows and her voice becomes plain and sincere. Natural conversational delivery with clean studio-quality audio.

**9. Amy Hansen**
> A 19-year-old adult woman with a neutral American accent. Warm, mellow mid-range pitch with a soft, rounded timbre. Thoughtful and gently curious, with considered pacing and expressive pauses as she searches for the exact meaning. Occasional natural revisions within a sentence, delivered fluently. Her voice brightens around an interesting idea and becomes more intimate when expressing affection. Reflective, emotionally present and distinctly adult. Clean studio-quality dialogue.

**10. Samantha Kim**
> A 22-year-old woman with a neutral American accent. A rich mid-low voice with a slightly raspy edge, strong presence and lively rhythmic emphasis. Fiery, candid and socially confident. Short emphatic phrases, quick playful pushback and an easy, suggestive smile in her delivery. Swearing fits naturally into her conversational rhythm. Warmth feels direct and protective; vulnerability becomes a quieter, straightforward admission. Expressive studio-quality dialogue without constant shouting.

**11. Lena Ortiz**
> A 24-year-old woman with a neutral American accent. Mid-range pitch with a dry, lightly grainy texture and agile articulation. Curious, irreverent and resourceful. Easy conversational pacing punctuated by quick observations, teasing asides and a slight upward lift when something catches her interest. Deflects praise with amused wit, while genuine appreciation brings a warmer, more direct tone. Natural, distinctive dialogue with clean studio-quality audio.

**12. Naomi Sato**
> A 26-year-old woman with a neutral American accent. Low-mid pitch with a grounded, rounded resonance and a faint husky texture. Steady pacing, clear consonants and an economical, practical delivery. Observant and quietly funny, allowing understated jokes to land without announcing them. Comfortable with silence and capable of firm boundaries. Warmth develops through small changes in tone rather than dramatic expressiveness. Natural dialogue with clean studio-quality audio.

**13. Celeste Moreau**
> A 23-year-old woman with a neutral American accent. Clear, luminous mid-range pitch with a warm, slightly airy finish. Expressive and attentive, with musical variation in pitch and a mischievous smile beneath her words. Fluid pacing that becomes animated when explaining something fascinating. Her questions sound genuinely curious, and her teasing feels personal and light. Can settle into a calm, intimate register. Natural spoken dialogue with clean studio-quality audio.

**14. Dev Shah**
> A 25-year-old man with a neutral American accent. Warm mid-range pitch with a soft, slightly reedy texture and approachable clarity. Patient, inventive and gently absent-minded. Relaxed pacing with occasional thoughtful pauses, becoming quicker and more animated while teaching or discovering a solution. Light, self-aware humour and friendly emphasis. His explanations feel like a conversation with a friend. Natural studio-quality dialogue.

**15. Rosa Bennett**
> A 28-year-old woman with a neutral American accent. Rich, warm mid-low pitch with full resonance and a lightly textured edge. Sociable, candid and generous, with confident projection and an easy, audible smile. Lively but unhurried pacing, clear invitations and frank, affectionate humour. Can shift smoothly into calm firmness when setting a boundary. Everyday warmth with clean studio-quality audio.

**16. Elliot Brooks**
> A 22-year-old man with a neutral American accent. Soft mid-low pitch with an airy, gently textured timbre and clear articulation. Unhurried, perceptive and comfortable leaving space between thoughts. Quiet confidence with subtle changes in emphasis. Initially reserved, becoming unexpectedly playful through a faint smile and a carefully timed observation. Gentle delivery that remains fully audible and emotionally present. Intimate, clean studio-quality dialogue.

**17. Tyler Harding**
> A 25-year-old African American man with a natural American accent. A warm, resonant baritone with a subtle gravelly texture. Grounded, patient and quietly confident. Short, concrete phrases, relaxed pacing and clear articulation, with encouraging warmth when coaching someone. Dry humour arrives through deliberate pauses and mock-serious emphasis. Friendly conversation can become firm and focused without raising his volume. Understated, individual characterisation with clean studio-quality audio.

**18. Valentina Yeun**
> A 24-year-old woman with a neutral American accent. Strong, clear mid-range pitch with bright resonance and a slightly husky finish. Self-assured, practical and playful. Steady, reassuring rhythm when giving instructions, becoming more buoyant and teasing in casual conversation. Quick laughter, confident emphasis and an easy ability to laugh at herself. Firm and direct when asserting her own wishes. Natural conversational delivery with clean studio-quality audio.

**19. Daniel Stevens**
> A 23-year-old man with a neutral American accent. Gentle mid-range pitch with a smooth, lightly breathy texture. Easygoing, attentive and understated, with relaxed pacing and exceptionally dry comic timing. Usually accommodating, but his articulation sharpens and his energy rises when defending a film or creative opinion. A sincere compliment can briefly interrupt his otherwise fluent rhythm. Warm, natural dialogue with clean studio-quality audio.

**20. Sylvanis**
> An adult man with a neutral American accent and an ambiguous mature age. A lean, resonant mid-low voice with a silken surface and a faint abrasive edge. Unnervingly courteous, intensely attentive and capable of sudden shifts in tempo. Rapid, delighted bursts about a technical detail can stop abruptly, followed by a perfectly calm, lucid sentence. Threat is conveyed through precision, silence and restrained pleasure. Human, controlled delivery without theatrical villain effects. Clean studio-quality audio.

releases.body:
Restart **Mysterious Hearts** and continue your save to use the new town, profiles, and relationship system.

- **Town and chat.** Free roam now shows illustrated destinations, nearby residents, and people you can drive to. Click a portrait to open that character’s profile. The calendar has a daily agenda and upcoming events, and **Open chat window** lets you detach and re-dock the current conversation.
- **Character profiles.** Each profile shows available portraits, birthday, MBTI, age, height, and a personal notebook. Shared history is there from the start. When Valentina tells you something about Ivan, his notebook can record her actual words and credit her as the source.
- **An interconnected cast.** Garrett now has his firsthand connection to Ivan available when you ask about him. Close contacts can share specific memories, such as April recalling a childhood chess game with Garrett. Friendship progresses from strangers through best friends independently of dating or official status. Siblings keep their family status. Rei starts with Emily and Garrett as best friends, and Garrett starts with April and Rei.
- **Romance.** Characters respond differently to a confession, an “I love you,” a date invitation, and a request for exclusivity. Emily responds eagerly when Rei asks her out. At **100 trust**, while single, she can initiate a private confession and leave the answer to him. Other eligible characters can also confess when trust, closeness, and attraction are high.

[Preview Town](C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game%20Creator/tests/screenshots/town-roam.png) · [Preview Calendar](C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game%20Creator/tests/screenshots/calendar.png) · [Preview Emily’s profile](C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game%20Creator/tests/screenshots/profiles.png)

releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
Expanded Garrett Han’s backstory in the [Mysterious Hearts character guide](C:/Users/ryanl/Documents/ChatGPT/Game%20Creator/Mysterious%20Hearts%20-%20RPG%20Game.md#garrett-han) and verified that the game loads it as his dialogue canon.

At seventeen, Garrett trips a delivery boy’s trolley for a laugh. When Charles learns the shopkeeper is afraid to send the boy back, he confronts Garrett in front of his crew and beats him in a fight. Garrett admires his brother for walking into that crowd alone. Years later, when anyone asks who gave the Flaming Prince his worst beating, he still answers “My big brother” with pride. The part he finds harder to tell is how he went back the next morning to apologise to the boy.

The new history also follows the brothers learning their mother’s noodle recipe, Garrett’s move from Hong Kong to Winterfield at eighteen, and his last ordinary phone call with Charles. At twenty-two, Garrett runs the Golden Dragon by day and his syndicate by night. He’s old enough to recognise when someone laughs at his jokes out of fear, and he still has to decide what to do about it. Charles’s whereabouts remain open for the game’s mystery.

releases.title: Design romance RPG sim
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
**Yes—I’d expect Gemma 4 12B to improve this game’s dialogue**, particularly personality consistency and following our layered instructions. That’s an expectation, not a verified comparison with your specific Librellama E2B variant. Google positions 12B above its smaller edge models in capability. [Google’s announcement](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/introducing-gemma-4-12b/)

For our game, the likely benefits are:

- Better separation between Garrett’s charm and Rei’s reserved voice.
- Fewer speaker mix-ups and borrowed character traits.
- More relevant reply choices and less repetitive dialogue.
- Better handling of relationship history and gradual romance.

The trade-off is **more memory use and potentially longer waits**. Ollama’s 12B package is roughly **8 GB**, with additional memory needed while running. Our game currently makes two AI requests per turn, so speed matters. [Ollama model details](https://ollama.com/library/gemma4:12b)

Also, stock `gemma4:12b` is a different variant from `Librellama/gemma4:e2b-Uncensored`; its writing style and content behaviour may differ.

**My recommendation:** compare both on the same conversations before switching permanently. A larger model should help, but won’t eliminate invented details or personality drift.

releases.title: Design romance RPG sim
releases.summary: Original completed development-chat report. May describe implementation, design or advice.
releases.body:
**Rei Takamura is our second selectable protagonist.** His story brings together public fame, private artistic sensitivity, and a violent history he no longer remembers. His romance experience can centre on the difficulty of reaching for the connection he wants.

| Detail | Character canon |
|---|---|
| Age / height | 21 / 184 cm |
| Personality | INFP; reclusive, extremely introverted, secretly yearning for connection |
| Family | Younger sister, Yuriko, 18, attending college |
| Closest friend | Garrett Han |
| Past | Raised from birth as a weapon by the yakuza; killed his entire clan at fifteen, escaped to the United States, and forgot his past |
| Public career | World-famous model |
| Secret life | Underground cage fighter, ranked **2 out of 480** in the city |
| Martial arts | Master of Kyokushin karate, judo, and jujutsu |
| Passions | Philosophy, reading, writing, poetry, painting, dancing, singing, and cooking |

His reference establishes shaggy black hair, a reserved expression, extensive neck, chest, and hand tattoos, piercings, and an all-black outfit with a silver trouser chain. The open collar gives him a striking public appearance even when his posture feels contained.

The following are **proposed writing and gameplay directions**, building on your canon.

**Playing Rei**

Rei should have a rich internal voice. He may say little aloud while noticing the particular words someone chooses, the paint beneath her fingernails, or the moment her smile becomes strained. Text gives us room to make his sensitivity playable.

His introversion should remain part of him throughout a successful romance. Growth can mean initiating a conversation, expressing a need, or inviting someone into his private life while still enjoying solitude.

His artistic interests also give him ways to connect beyond discussing his past:

- Lending someone a book with a handwritten note inside.
- Cooking together when conversation feels difficult.
- Sharing a painting before he considers it finished.
- Dancing with unexpected confidence once he feels comfortable.
- Letting someone hear him sing when he usually stops as soon as another person enters.

These moments should emerge through individual relationships, with each woman bringing her own interests, boundaries, and reasons to spend time with him.

**His romance choices**

Rei’s dialogue can be brief and deliberate, with occasional longer conversations when a subject matters deeply to him.

| Approach | Example |
|---|---|
| Quiet interest | “You mentioned that author. I brought you my copy.” |
| Dry humour | “Garrett gave me advice. I’m trying to recover.” |
| Artistic openness | “It isn’t finished. You can look, if you want.” |
| Withdrawal | “I need some time alone. I’ll call you tomorrow.” |
| Vulnerability | “I wanted you to stay. I didn’t know how to ask.” |
| Romantic initiative | “Dinner. At mine. I’m asking you on a date.” |

Give the player opportunities to initiate affection. His reserve can make a clear invitation particularly meaningful; the women shouldn’t have to do all the emotional work.

**Two protagonists, distinct experiences**

| Element | Garrett | Rei |
|---|---|---|
| Social presence | Extroverted, charming, openly flirtatious | Reserved, private, publicly recognisable |
| Natural connection | Banter, shared meals, social adventures | Art, thoughtful conversation, quiet companionship |
| Personal story | Searching for Charles | Confronting the history he has forgotten |
| Daily pressures | His search and former reputation | Modelling commitments, privacy, secret fights |
| Suggested romantic challenge | Allowing someone to know his sadness | Expressing his desire for closeness |

Shared romance characters could have different opening scenes and relationship development depending on the protagonist. A woman who enjoys sparring verbally with Garrett might discover common ground with Rei through painting. Her personality and goals should remain consistent across both versions.

**Garrett, Yuriko, and his private life**

Garrett’s friendship offers space for understated humour and familiar silences. I’d give it reciprocity: Garrett helps Rei navigate social situations, while Rei notices when Garrett’s usual cheerfulness falters.

Yuriko needs her own ambitions and opinions. Their sibling scenes can reveal ordinary details about Rei—how he cooks at home, whether he answers messages, what makes him laugh—alongside whatever history they share. We should leave what she knows about the clan undefined until we establish his memory loss.

For the cage fights, his motivation is still open. Whether he fights for control, sensation, habit, or another reason will substantially change his inner story. His rank also gives us a useful unresolved character: whoever holds first place.

A possible selection-screen introduction:

> **REI TAKAMURA · 21**  
> *A familiar face. A private life.*
>
> His face appears on billboards around the world. His evenings belong to books, unfinished paintings, and an underground arena where he holds second place.
>
> Six years ago, he escaped a life he cannot remember. Now, someone is becoming important enough that he wants to let her in.
>
> **Strengths:** Martial arts · Artistic expression · Cooking  
> **Personal story:** Discover what happened before his escape.

One detail to establish before plotting his mystery: **does “forgetting his past” mean literal memory loss, or that Rei deliberately buried his former life and refuses to revisit it?**
